notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • LASER stands for Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation.
  • A laser produces a highly directional, coherent and nearly monochromatic beam of light.
  • Laser light is produced by stimulated emission.
  • Laser action requires an active medium, energy source and optical resonator in most conventional lasers.
  • Population inversion is essential for sustained laser amplification.
  • Lasers can operate in continuous-wave or pulsed mode.
  • Laser radiation may lie in the ultraviolet, visible or infrared region depending on the laser type.
  • Laser light is electromagnetic radiation.
  • Laser beams can carry large amounts of energy in a very narrow beam.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

LASER → Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation

2. Important Properties of Laser Light

Main properties are:

  • High coherence.
  • High directionality.
  • Very low divergence.
  • Nearly monochromatic nature.
  • High intensity.
  • High brightness.
  • Ability to focus into a very small spot.
📌 Must-Memorise

Laser → Coherent + Directional + Nearly Monochromatic + Intense

3. Monochromatic Light
  • Monochromatic light has a very narrow range of wavelengths.
  • Laser light is much more nearly monochromatic than ordinary lamp light.
  • Different lasers emit at different characteristic wavelengths.
  • Monochromaticity makes lasers useful in spectroscopy and precision measurement.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Monochromatic → Nearly Single Wavelength

4. Coherence
  • Coherent waves maintain a stable phase relationship.
  • Laser light has high temporal and spatial coherence.
  • Coherence enables strong interference effects.
  • Holography depends on coherent light.
  • Ordinary light sources generally have much lower coherence.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Coherence → Fixed Phase Relationship

5. Directionality
  • Laser beams are highly directional.
  • They spread much less than ordinary light beams.
  • This property is called low divergence.
  • Laser beams can travel long distances while remaining narrow.
  • Directionality is useful in communication, surveying and range finding.
6. High Intensity
  • Laser energy can be concentrated into a narrow beam.
  • A laser beam can be focused to a very small spot.
  • This produces very high power density.
  • High intensity allows cutting, welding and surgery.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Laser Focus → Very High Power Density

7. Ordinary Light vs Laser Light
  • Ordinary light is generally incoherent.
  • Laser light is highly coherent.
  • Ordinary light spreads in many directions.
  • Laser light is highly directional.
  • Ordinary light contains a broad range of wavelengths.
  • Laser light has a much narrower wavelength range.
  • Laser beams can be much more intense.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Laser light is not simply “brighter ordinary light”; its coherence and directionality are distinctive.

8. Atomic Energy Levels
  • Electrons in atoms and molecules occupy discrete energy states.
  • They can move between energy levels by absorbing or emitting energy.
  • A transition from a higher energy level to a lower level can emit a photon.
  • Photon energy equals the difference between the two energy levels.
📌 Formula

E₂ − E₁ = hf

9. Absorption
  • Absorption occurs when an atom absorbs a photon.
  • The photon energy must match an allowed energy difference.
  • An electron is promoted from a lower energy state to a higher energy state.
  • Absorption is one of the processes involved in laser pumping.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Absorption → Lower Level to Higher Level

10. Spontaneous Emission
  • An excited atom can return to a lower energy level spontaneously.
  • It emits a photon.
  • The emitted photon has energy equal to the level difference.
  • The emission direction and phase are generally random.
  • Ordinary lamps contain large amounts of spontaneous emission.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Spontaneous Emission → Random Phase/Direction

11. Stimulated Emission
  • Stimulated emission occurs when an incoming photon interacts with an excited atom.
  • The atom is stimulated to drop to a lower energy level.
  • A second photon is emitted.
  • The emitted photon has the same frequency as the stimulating photon.
  • It also has the same phase, direction and polarisation under ideal treatment.
  • This process produces optical amplification.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Stimulated Emission → Identical Coherent Photon

12. Einstein and Stimulated Emission
  • Albert Einstein introduced the theoretical concept of stimulated emission in 1917.
  • He described absorption, spontaneous emission and stimulated emission using Einstein coefficients.
  • Stimulated emission later became the physical basis of masers and lasers.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Einstein → Stimulated Emission → 1917

13. Population Inversion
  • Normally, more atoms occupy lower energy states than higher ones.
  • Laser action requires more particles in an excited laser level than in the lower laser level.
  • This condition is called population inversion.
  • Population inversion is a non-equilibrium state.
  • Without population inversion, absorption would dominate over stimulated emission.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Population Inversion → More Atoms in Upper Laser Level

14. Pumping
  • Pumping supplies energy to the active medium.
  • Pumping creates population inversion.
  • Pumping may be optical, electrical or chemical.
  • Flash lamps can optically pump some lasers.
  • Electrical discharge pumps many gas lasers.
  • Electric current pumps semiconductor lasers.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Pumping → Creates Population Inversion

15. Active Medium
  • The active medium is the material in which stimulated emission and amplification occur.
  • It may be solid, liquid, gas or semiconductor.
  • Ruby is a solid-state laser medium.
  • Helium-neon is a gas-laser system.
  • Semiconductor junctions form the active region of laser diodes.
16. Metastable State
  • A metastable state is an excited state with a relatively long lifetime.
  • It allows atoms to remain excited long enough to build population inversion.
  • Metastable states are important in many laser systems.
  • Ruby laser action relies on a metastable energy level.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Metastable State → Helps Population Inversion

17. Optical Resonator
  • A typical laser contains two mirrors around the active medium.
  • One mirror is highly reflecting.
  • The other is partially transmitting.
  • Light reflects repeatedly between mirrors.
  • Repeated passage through the active medium causes amplification.
  • Part of the amplified beam emerges through the partially reflecting mirror.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Laser Cavity → Two Mirrors

18. Laser Resonator Mirrors
  • One mirror ideally reflects nearly all incident laser light.
  • The second mirror is called the output coupler.
  • The output coupler allows a fraction of the beam to escape.
  • Multiple reflections enhance stimulated emission.
19. Basic Laser Components

A conventional laser generally contains:

  • Active medium.
  • Pumping source.
  • Optical resonator.
  • Highly reflecting mirror.
  • Partially reflecting output mirror.
📌 Must-Memorise

Laser = Active Medium + Pump + Resonator

20. Working Principle — Basic Sequence
  • Pump energy is supplied.
  • Atoms or carriers are excited.
  • Population inversion develops.
  • A photon triggers stimulated emission.
  • Identical photons stimulate further emissions.
  • Light is amplified in the resonator.
  • A coherent laser beam emerges through the output coupler.
21. Three-Level Laser
  • A three-level laser uses three principal energy levels.
  • Pumping excites particles from ground level to a high level.
  • They rapidly fall to a metastable level.
  • Laser transition occurs from metastable level to the ground or lower level.
  • Ruby laser is a classic three-level laser.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ruby Laser → Three-Level Laser

22. Four-Level Laser
  • A four-level laser uses four principal energy levels.
  • The lower laser level lies above the ground state.
  • It empties quickly.
  • Population inversion is easier to maintain than in many three-level systems.
  • Many practical lasers use four-level schemes.
23. Ruby Laser
  • Ruby laser was the first successful laser.
  • It was demonstrated by Theodore H. Maiman in 1960.
  • Ruby is aluminium oxide containing chromium ions.
  • Chromium ions act as active centres.
  • Ruby laser emits deep red light.
  • Its wavelength is about 694.3 nm.
  • It is a solid-state laser.
  • Ruby laser commonly operates in pulsed mode.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

First Laser → Ruby Laser → Theodore Maiman → 1960

24. Ruby Composition
  • Ruby is aluminium oxide, Al₂O₃, doped with small amounts of chromium.
  • Chromium ions are responsible for laser action.
  • Synthetic ruby rods are commonly used in ruby lasers.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ruby Laser → Al₂O₃ + Cr³⁺

25. Ruby Laser Pumping
  • Ruby lasers are commonly optically pumped.
  • A flash lamp surrounds or lies close to the ruby rod.
  • Light from the lamp excites chromium ions.
  • Population inversion develops in a metastable state.
26. Helium-Neon Laser
  • Helium-neon laser is a gas laser.
  • Its active gas mixture contains helium and neon.
  • Electrical discharge excites helium atoms.
  • Energy transfer from helium helps excite neon.
  • Neon provides the main laser transition.
  • A common visible He-Ne laser wavelength is 632.8 nm.
  • It emits red light.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

He-Ne Laser → Gas Laser → 632.8 nm Red

27. Helium's Role in He-Ne Laser
  • Helium atoms are excited by electrical discharge.
  • Excited helium transfers energy to neon atoms through collisions.
  • This helps create population inversion in neon.
  • Neon then produces laser emission.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

In a He-Ne laser, neon is the main species responsible for the common laser emission.

28. Carbon Dioxide Laser
  • CO₂ laser is a gas laser.
  • It commonly emits infrared radiation.
  • A major wavelength is around 10.6 μm.
  • CO₂ lasers can have high efficiency and high power.
  • They are widely used for industrial cutting and welding.
  • They are also used in some medical procedures.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

CO₂ Laser → Infrared → Industrial Cutting

29. Nd:YAG Laser
  • Nd:YAG stands for neodymium-doped yttrium aluminium garnet.
  • It is a solid-state laser.
  • A common emission wavelength is 1064 nm.
  • This lies in the near-infrared.
  • Nd:YAG lasers are used in industry, medicine and range finding.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Nd:YAG → Solid-State → 1064 nm

30. Semiconductor Laser
  • Semiconductor laser is also called a laser diode.
  • It uses a semiconductor p-n junction or related heterostructure.
  • Electrical current injects charge carriers.
  • Recombination produces photons.
  • Stimulated emission creates laser light.
  • Semiconductor lasers are compact and efficient.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Laser Diode → Semiconductor Laser

31. Materials Used in Laser Diodes
  • Gallium arsenide is an important semiconductor-laser material.
  • Compound semiconductors are widely used.
  • Different semiconductor compositions produce different wavelengths.
  • Laser diodes are used in optical communication and optical-disc systems.
32. Dye Laser
  • Dye lasers use organic dye solutions as the active medium.
  • They are usually optically pumped.
  • Dye lasers can be tuned across a range of wavelengths.
  • Tunability makes them useful in spectroscopy and research.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Dye Laser → Tunable Laser

33. Excimer Laser
  • Excimer lasers commonly operate in the ultraviolet region.
  • They use excited molecular complexes.
  • They can produce short-wavelength high-energy pulses.
  • Excimer lasers are used in photolithography and eye surgery.
  • LASIK commonly uses an excimer laser to reshape the cornea.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Excimer Laser → UV → LASIK

34. Fibre Laser
  • Fibre lasers use an optical fibre doped with rare-earth ions as the active medium.
  • Ytterbium, erbium and neodymium are common dopants.
  • Fibre lasers have efficient heat dissipation.
  • They are widely used in industrial cutting and marking.
35. Continuous-Wave Laser
  • Continuous-wave lasers produce a nearly continuous output beam.
  • Output power remains relatively steady over time.
  • Many He-Ne lasers operate in continuous-wave mode.
  • Continuous lasers are useful in alignment and communication.
36. Pulsed Laser
  • Pulsed lasers emit energy in short bursts.
  • Pulses can have very high peak power.
  • Ruby lasers commonly produce pulses.
  • Pulsed lasers are used in range finding, surgery and material processing.
37. Laser Wavelength and Colour
  • A laser's wavelength depends on transitions in its active medium.
  • Ruby laser → about 694 nm.
  • He-Ne → about 632.8 nm.
  • Nd:YAG → about 1064 nm.
  • CO₂ → about 10.6 μm.
  • Excimer lasers often operate in ultraviolet.
38. Maser
  • MASER stands for Microwave Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation.
  • Maser uses stimulated emission in the microwave region.
  • Maser development preceded the laser.
  • Charles Townes made major contributions to the maser.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

MASER → Microwave

LASER → Light

39. First Maser
  • The first practical maser was developed in the 1950s.
  • Charles Townes and colleagues were central to its development.
  • The maser established stimulated-emission amplification before optical lasers became practical.
40. Charles Townes
  • Charles H. Townes was a major pioneer of maser and laser physics.
  • He shared the 1964 Nobel Prize in Physics with Nikolay Basov and Alexander Prokhorov.
  • Their work laid theoretical and experimental foundations for quantum electronics.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Townes + Basov + Prokhorov → Maser/Laser Physics

41. Theodore Maiman
  • Theodore H. Maiman built the first working laser.
  • He used a synthetic ruby crystal.
  • The first successful laser operation was achieved in 1960.
  • The laser emitted pulsed red light.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Maiman → First Working Laser → 1960

42. Laser Beam Divergence
  • Divergence is the spreading angle of a beam.
  • Laser beams have very small divergence.
  • Low divergence allows long-distance targeting and communication.
  • Beam divergence is not exactly zero.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Laser beam is highly directional, but it does not remain perfectly parallel forever.

43. Coherence Length
  • Coherence length is the distance over which a wave maintains a predictable phase relationship.
  • Lasers can have long coherence lengths compared with ordinary sources.
  • High coherence is useful for interferometry and holography.
44. Interferometry
  • Interferometry uses interference of coherent waves for precise measurement.
  • Lasers are ideal sources because of their coherence.
  • Interferometers can measure extremely small length changes.
  • They are used in metrology, engineering and scientific research.
45. Holography
  • Holography records both amplitude and phase information of light through interference.
  • Laser light is commonly used because of its coherence.
  • A hologram can reproduce a three-dimensional appearance.
  • Dennis Gabor developed the principle of holography.
  • Gabor received the 1971 Nobel Prize in Physics.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Dennis Gabor → Holography → Nobel 1971

46. Hologram
  • A hologram is an interference pattern recorded from object and reference beams.
  • When illuminated appropriately, it reconstructs the wavefront from the object.
  • It can provide depth information.
  • Holograms are used in security labels and optical applications.
47. Laser in Optical-Fibre Communication
  • Semiconductor lasers are widely used as optical sources.
  • Laser light is coupled into optical fibres.
  • Information modulates the optical signal.
  • Optical fibres provide high bandwidth.
  • Laser directionality and high modulation speed make them suitable for communication.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Optical Communication → Laser Diode + Optical Fibre

48. Laser in CD/DVD/Blu-ray
  • Optical-disc systems use lasers to read stored information.
  • Compact discs use infrared/near-infrared laser systems in common implementations.
  • DVDs use shorter-wavelength red lasers.
  • Blu-ray systems use even shorter-wavelength blue-violet lasers.
  • Shorter wavelength allows smaller data features and greater storage density.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Shorter Wavelength → Higher Optical-Disc Storage Density

49. Barcode Scanner
  • Laser scanners can illuminate barcodes with a narrow beam.
  • Reflected light differs between dark and light regions.
  • A detector converts reflected patterns into electrical signals.
  • Many modern barcode readers also use LEDs or imaging systems.
50. Laser Printer
  • Laser printers use a laser or laser-like scanning optical system to create an electrostatic image on a photoconductive drum.
  • Toner is attracted to selected charged regions.
  • The toner image is transferred to paper.
  • Heat fixes the toner onto the paper.
51. Laser Range Finder
  • A laser range finder sends a laser pulse toward a target.
  • The reflected pulse returns to the detector.
  • Distance can be calculated from travel time.
  • d = ct/2 for a pulse travelling through air approximately at c.
  • Division by 2 accounts for the outward and return path.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Laser Range → Distance = ct/2

52. LIDAR
  • LIDAR stands for Light Detection and Ranging.
  • It uses laser pulses to measure distance.
  • It can create three-dimensional maps.
  • It is used in surveying, autonomous systems, atmospheric studies and topographic mapping.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

LIDAR → Light Detection and Ranging

53. RADAR vs LIDAR
  • RADAR generally uses radio or microwave electromagnetic waves.
  • LIDAR uses laser light.
  • Both can use travel time and reflection to determine distance.
  • LIDAR can provide very high spatial resolution under suitable conditions.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

RADAR → Radio/Microwave.

LIDAR → Laser Light.

54. Laser in Surveying
  • Laser levels provide straight reference lines.
  • Laser distance meters measure distance precisely.
  • Surveyors use lasers for alignment and elevation measurements.
  • Construction industries use laser-based levelling systems.
55. Laser in Industry

Major industrial applications include:

  • Cutting.
  • Welding.
  • Drilling.
  • Engraving.
  • Marking.
  • Surface treatment.
  • Precision measurement.
  • Additive manufacturing.
56. Laser Cutting
  • A focused high-power laser heats material intensely.
  • Material may melt, burn or vaporise.
  • A gas jet may remove molten material.
  • Laser cutting provides high precision and narrow cuts.
57. Laser Welding
  • Laser welding concentrates energy into a small region.
  • It can produce deep narrow welds.
  • It is used in automobile, electronics and precision manufacturing.
  • Minimal contact is required.
58. Laser Drilling
  • Pulsed lasers can remove material from tiny areas.
  • Very small holes can be produced.
  • Laser drilling is used in electronics and precision engineering.
59. Laser Engraving
  • Laser energy modifies or removes surface material.
  • It produces permanent markings.
  • It is used for serial numbers, codes and designs.
60. Laser in Medicine

Applications include:

  • Eye surgery.
  • Skin treatment.
  • Dental procedures.
  • Tumour treatment in selected applications.
  • Cutting and cauterising tissue.
  • Kidney-stone treatment in some laser procedures.
61. LASIK
  • LASIK stands for Laser-Assisted In Situ Keratomileusis.
  • It is a refractive eye-surgery procedure.
  • An excimer laser reshapes corneal tissue.
  • It can correct selected cases of myopia, hypermetropia and astigmatism.
  • Patient suitability must be assessed clinically.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

LASIK → Excimer Laser → Cornea

62. Laser Photocoagulation
  • Lasers can coagulate tissue and blood vessels.
  • In ophthalmology, laser photocoagulation is used in selected retinal conditions.
  • Laser energy creates controlled thermal effects in tissue.
63. Laser in Dermatology
  • Lasers can remove tattoos and pigmented lesions.
  • They can reduce unwanted hair.
  • Different wavelengths target different tissue chromophores.
  • Pulsed lasers can selectively deliver energy.
64. Laser in Dentistry
  • Lasers may be used in certain soft-tissue dental procedures.
  • Some systems can assist cutting or ablation.
  • Lasers can reduce bleeding because of coagulation in suitable procedures.
  • Use depends on laser wavelength and dental application.
65. Laser Lithotripsy
  • Laser energy can fragment urinary stones.
  • Holmium:YAG lasers are commonly used in urological stone treatment.
  • A flexible optical fibre can deliver the laser energy to the stone.
66. Laser in Cancer Treatment
  • Lasers may destroy or remove selected superficial or accessible tumours.
  • Photodynamic therapy may use laser light to activate a photosensitive drug.
  • Lasers can also be used surgically to cut and coagulate tissue.
67. Photodynamic Therapy
  • A photosensitising drug is administered.
  • The drug accumulates preferentially in selected tissue in some treatments.
  • Light of a suitable wavelength activates the drug.
  • Reactive chemical species damage targeted cells.
  • Lasers can provide the activating light.
68. Laser in Eye Retina
  • Laser beams can be focused precisely onto retinal tissue.
  • Controlled photocoagulation can seal abnormal blood vessels or treat selected retinal disorders.
  • Precision is possible because laser light can be tightly focused.
69. Military Applications
  • Laser range finders measure target distance.
  • Laser designators mark targets.
  • Lasers are used in guidance and alignment systems.
  • High-power laser research also exists for directed-energy applications.
  • Military use is strictly regulated.
70. Laser in Astronomy
  • Lasers are used in adaptive optics.
  • Laser guide stars help correct atmospheric distortion.
  • Lunar laser ranging measures the Earth-Moon distance precisely.
  • Reflectors placed on the Moon return laser pulses.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Lunar Laser Ranging → Precise Earth-Moon Distance

71. Laser Cooling
  • Laser cooling uses photon momentum to slow atoms.
  • It can cool atomic gases to extremely low temperatures.
  • It is used in atomic clocks and quantum experiments.
  • Laser cooling helped make Bose-Einstein condensates possible.
72. Laser Trapping
  • Focused laser beams can exert small forces on microscopic particles.
  • Optical tweezers use light to trap and manipulate particles.
  • Arthur Ashkin pioneered optical trapping.
  • He received part of the 2018 Nobel Prize in Physics.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Optical Tweezers → Arthur Ashkin

73. Atomic Clock Link
  • Lasers are used to interrogate precise atomic transitions.
  • Highly stable laser frequencies improve precision.
  • Modern optical atomic clocks use laser-controlled atoms or ions.
74. Laser Spectroscopy
  • Laser spectroscopy studies interaction of laser light with matter.
  • Narrow linewidth allows precise energy-level measurements.
  • It is used to identify atoms and molecules.
  • It has applications in chemistry, physics and environmental monitoring.
75. Raman Spectroscopy
  • Raman spectroscopy studies inelastic scattering of light.
  • Lasers are commonly used as intense monochromatic sources.
  • Raman effect was discovered by C. V. Raman in 1928.
  • Raman spectroscopy identifies molecular vibrational information.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Laser + Raman Spectroscopy → C. V. Raman

76. Laser in Metrology
  • Laser wavelength provides a stable measurement reference.
  • Interferometers can measure tiny distances.
  • Lasers are used in calibration and dimensional measurement.
  • Precision manufacturing uses laser metrology.
77. Laser Gyroscope
  • Ring laser gyroscopes use interference of counter-propagating laser beams.
  • Rotation produces a measurable frequency difference through the Sagnac effect.
  • They are used in inertial navigation systems.
78. Laser Safety — Basic Facts
  • Laser beams can damage the eye.
  • High-power lasers can burn skin.
  • Reflected beams can also be hazardous.
  • Invisible infrared and ultraviolet lasers are especially dangerous because the eye may not perceive the beam.
  • Protective eyewear must match the laser wavelength.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Laser Hazard → Eye Damage

79. Eye Hazard
  • The eye can focus visible and near-infrared laser light onto the retina.
  • This can produce very high intensity at the retinal surface.
  • Retinal burns may cause permanent vision loss.
  • Looking directly into a laser beam is unsafe.
80. Laser Classes
  • Lasers are classified according to potential hazard.
  • Low-power consumer laser products may belong to lower hazard classes.
  • High-power industrial and medical lasers require strict controls.
  • Exact classification depends on wavelength, power and exposure conditions.
81. Laser Pointer Safety
  • Laser pointers should never be aimed at eyes.
  • They should not be aimed at aircraft.
  • Even low-power visible lasers can cause glare and temporary visual disturbance.
  • Higher-power unregulated pointers can cause permanent eye injury.
82. Laser vs LED
  • LED emits light mainly through spontaneous emission.
  • Laser diode uses stimulated emission.
  • LED light is less coherent.
  • Laser light is more directional and spectrally narrow.
  • LEDs generally have broader emission angles.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

LED → Spontaneous Emission

Laser → Stimulated Emission

83. Laser Diode vs LED in Communication
  • Laser diodes provide higher optical intensity.
  • They allow faster modulation.
  • They have narrower spectral width.
  • LEDs can be cheaper and simpler.
  • Long-distance high-capacity fibre links commonly use laser sources.
84. Laser Efficiency
  • Efficiency is output laser energy divided by input energy.
  • Different laser types have very different efficiencies.
  • Semiconductor lasers can be highly efficient.
  • Some early solid-state lasers such as ruby have relatively low efficiency.
85. Optical Pumping
  • Optical pumping uses light to excite the active medium.
  • Flash lamps pump ruby lasers.
  • Other lasers may be pumped by another laser.
  • Optical pumping helps create population inversion.
86. Electrical Pumping
  • Gas lasers often use electric discharge.
  • Semiconductor lasers use electric current injection.
  • Electrical pumping converts electrical energy into excitation of the active medium.
87. Chemical Laser
  • Chemical lasers obtain excitation energy from chemical reactions.
  • Some can produce very high output power.
  • They are less common in everyday applications.
88. Excited State
  • An excited state has higher energy than the ground state.
  • It is generally unstable.
  • An excited atom may lose energy by spontaneous or stimulated emission.
  • Laser systems use carefully chosen excited states.
89. Ground State
  • Ground state is the lowest-energy state of an atom or molecule.
  • Under ordinary thermal conditions, many particles occupy lower energy states.
  • Pumping moves particles away from the ground state.
90. Einstein Coefficients

Einstein described:

  • Absorption.
  • Spontaneous emission.
  • Stimulated emission.
  • These processes are represented using Einstein A and B coefficients.
  • The theory laid the foundation for laser physics.
91. Photon Multiplication
  • One stimulating photon can trigger emission of another matching photon.
  • Both can trigger further stimulated emissions.
  • This produces amplification.
  • The optical cavity repeatedly sends photons through the active medium.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Stimulated Emission → Chain Amplification of Photons

92. Why Laser Needs Population Inversion
  • If most particles are in the lower state, absorption dominates.
  • Population inversion allows stimulated emission to exceed absorption.
  • Net optical gain then becomes possible.
  • This is essential for laser oscillation.
93. Laser Threshold
  • Laser action begins only when optical gain exceeds total losses.
  • This condition is called threshold.
  • Below threshold, the device may emit mainly spontaneous light.
  • Above threshold, stimulated emission dominates.
94. Resonant Cavity
  • Only certain optical modes satisfy cavity resonance conditions.
  • The cavity helps select frequencies.
  • This contributes to narrow laser linewidth.
  • Cavity length influences longitudinal modes.
95. Laser Beam Focusing
  • A lens can focus a laser beam into a very small spot.
  • Smaller spot area gives greater power density.
  • Precision cutting and surgery exploit this property.
  • Diffraction ultimately limits the minimum focus size.
96. Laser and Diffraction
  • Laser beams still obey diffraction.
  • A perfectly non-diverging beam is impossible.
  • Beam divergence depends partly on wavelength and beam diameter.
  • Larger beam diameter can reduce diffraction-limited divergence.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Laser beams have low divergence, not zero divergence.

97. Polarisation of Laser Light
  • Many lasers produce strongly polarised output.
  • Polarisation depends on cavity design and active medium.
  • Polarised laser light is useful in optical measurements.
98. Laser Communication in Space
  • Laser communication can transmit large amounts of data.
  • Narrow beams reduce spreading.
  • Precise pointing is required.
  • Atmospheric clouds can interfere with ground-based optical links.
99. Free-Space Optical Communication
  • Laser beams can carry data through air or space without optical fibre.
  • This is called free-space optical communication.
  • It requires near line-of-sight.
  • Fog and atmospheric turbulence can reduce performance.
100. Laser in 3D Scanning
  • LIDAR can measure many distances rapidly.
  • Computer systems reconstruct 3D surfaces.
  • Applications include mapping, archaeology, forestry and autonomous vehicles.
101. Laser in Archaeology
  • Airborne LIDAR can map terrain beneath vegetation.
  • It can reveal ancient structures and landscape features.
  • Laser scanning produces high-resolution elevation models.
  • It is non-invasive.
102. Laser in Weather and Atmosphere
  • LIDAR can study clouds and aerosols.
  • Laser pulses are sent into the atmosphere.
  • Backscattered light provides information about particles and atmospheric layers.
  • Doppler LIDAR can measure wind velocity.
103. Laser in Nuclear Fusion Research
  • Very powerful pulsed lasers can compress and heat tiny fuel targets.
  • This is called inertial confinement fusion.
  • Deuterium and tritium are common fusion fuels in research.
  • Laser energy creates extreme temperature and pressure.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Inertial Confinement Fusion → High-Power Lasers

104. Laser-Induced Fluorescence
  • Laser light excites atoms or molecules.
  • They subsequently emit fluorescence.
  • The emitted spectrum reveals chemical information.
  • It is used in environmental sensing and analytical chemistry.
105. Laser Ablation
  • Intense laser pulses remove material from a surface.
  • The material may vaporise or form plasma.
  • Laser ablation is used in material analysis, surgery and manufacturing.
106. Laser-Induced Breakdown Spectroscopy
  • LIBS stands for Laser-Induced Breakdown Spectroscopy.
  • A high-energy laser pulse creates a tiny plasma on a sample.
  • Emitted light is analysed.
  • The elemental composition of the material can be determined.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

LIBS → Laser Plasma → Elemental Analysis

107. Laser in Precision Timing
  • Short laser pulses can measure extremely brief time intervals.
  • Femtosecond lasers produce pulses of order 10⁻¹⁵ s.
  • Ultrashort pulses are used in research, microscopy and material processing.
108. Femtosecond Laser
  • One femtosecond equals 10⁻¹⁵ s.
  • Femtosecond lasers produce ultrashort pulses.
  • Their very short duration allows high peak powers.
  • They are used in precision eye surgery and ultrafast science.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Femto → 10⁻¹⁵

109. Laser Cooling and Nobel Link
  • Steven Chu, Claude Cohen-Tannoudji and William D. Phillips shared the 1997 Nobel Prize in Physics.
  • They were honoured for methods to cool and trap atoms with laser light.
  • Laser cooling is central to modern atomic physics.
110. Chirped Pulse Amplification
  • Chirped pulse amplification allows generation of extremely intense ultrashort laser pulses.
  • Gérard Mourou and Donna Strickland developed this technique.
  • They shared part of the 2018 Nobel Prize in Physics.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Mourou + Strickland → Chirped Pulse Amplification

  • Photon energy → E = hf.
  • Photon energy → E = hc/λ.

  • Photon energy → joule or electronvolt.
  • Power → watt.

118. TNPSC Traps
  • LASER is an acronym.
  • Laser action is based on stimulated emission.
  • Einstein proposed stimulated emission before the first laser was built.
  • First working laser was built by Theodore Maiman in 1960.
  • Ruby laser is a solid-state laser.
  • He-Ne is a gas laser.
  • CO₂ laser emits mainly infrared radiation.
  • Laser diode is a semiconductor laser.
  • Population inversion is essential.
  • Pumping creates population inversion.
  • Metastable states help maintain inversion.
  • One resonator mirror is highly reflecting.
  • The other is partially transmitting.
  • Laser light is highly coherent.
  • Laser light is not perfectly monochromatic.
  • Laser beams have low divergence, not zero divergence.
  • Stimulated emitted photon matches the stimulating photon in frequency and phase.
  • Holography depends on coherence.
  • Optical-fibre communication commonly uses semiconductor lasers.
  • LIDAR uses laser light.
  • RADAR uses radio/microwave radiation.
  • LASIK commonly uses an excimer laser.
  • Laser pointers can damage eyes.
  • Invisible laser radiation can be especially dangerous.
  • LED primarily uses spontaneous emission; laser uses stimulated emission.
